readerTitle: Sold out by 11: where should a busy bakery grow next?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 빵집, 치과용 예약 앱) · 단원 개념 두 가지(성장의 네 가지 방향, 핵심과 인접 이동)를 적용
insight: 성장 아이디어는 '좋은가'보다 '지금 하는 일에서 몇 걸음 떨어져 있는가'로 먼저 줄 세운다.
misconception: 성장하려면 2호점이나 새 사업처럼 큰 한 방이 필요하다. 가까워 보이는 확장은 위험이 없다.

sources.text: Ansoff, H. I. (1957). Strategies for Diversification. Harvard Business Review. (성장 매트릭스: 시장 침투, 제품 개발, 시장 개발, 다각화)
Zook, C. (2001). Profit from the Core. Harvard Business School Press. (핵심 사업과 인접 영역 확장)
빵집과 예약 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 빵집(Ana)과 치과 예약 앱은 모두 가상 사례입니다. 오전 11시 품절, 오후 2시 품절 등의 시간은 설명용이며 실제 수치나 연구 결과가 아닙니다.
네 가지 성장 방향의 이름(market penetration, product development, market development, diversification)이 STR-07-01 개념 레슨의 용어와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
'핵심에서 몇 걸음 떨어져 있는가'를 세는 방식이 STR-07-02(Core and adjacent moves)의 설명과 일치하는지 확인하세요. Zook의 원래 틀은 고객, 제품, 채널, 역량 등 여러 축을 사용합니다.

cards.title: Sold out by 11 a.m.
body: Ana sells sourdough and pastries from one small shop. Most mornings there's a line out the door, and by 11 the shelves are empty.
Everyone has advice. Regulars say open a second shop. A café owner wants to buy her bread wholesale. Her sister says sell online. Every idea is growth, but they aren't the same size of bet.

image.label: Empty bakery shelves with a line still outside
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 오전 11시를 가리키는 벽시계, 텅 빈 빵 진열대, 유리문 밖에 아직 서 있는 손님 줄. 카운터 뒤 제빵사가 머리를 긁는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 간판 문구는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should Ana grow first?
body: Ana has one oven, two bakers and savings for one move this year. Which comes first?

options.text: Open a second shop across town with a café and lunch menu
options.feedback: New location, new customers and new products all at once. That's close to diversification, with three things to learn while the first shop still turns buyers away.

options.text: Add an earlier baking shift and a second oven so she stops selling out
options.feedback: This is market penetration: more of what already sells, to people already waiting for it. It's the move closest to her core, and the demand is proven.

options.text: Start supplying bread to local cafés
options.feedback: Same bread, new customers: market development. A sensible step, but it competes for oven time she doesn't have yet.

cards.title: Her ideas on one grid.
body: Two questions sort every option: is the product new, and are the customers new?

breakdown.label: Same bread, new customers
breakdown.detail: Wholesale to cafés, a weekend market stall

cards.callout: Risk usually rises as you move down this list.

cards.title: The empty shelf is a clue.
body: Of the **four ways to grow**, penetration is usually the cheapest, because the product and the customers are already proven. A shop that sells out by 11 is turning away people who already want what it makes.
Ana adds a 4 a.m. shift and a second oven. Now the bread lasts until 2 p.m. Only when the line stops growing does she need a bigger step.

image.label: Two-by-two grid with the bakery placed in the top-left box
image.brief: 2×2 격자 인포그래픽. 가로축 "Same customers / New customers", 세로축 "Same products / New products". 왼쪽 위 칸(Penetration)에 빵 아이콘과 별표 강조, 나머지 칸에 샌드위치, 카페 납품 트럭, 새 매장 아이콘을 작게 배치.

cards.title: Bread now lasts until 2 p.m. What's next?
body: Ana wants a second move. Each option below is real growth. Before picking, count what each one asks her to learn.

options.text: Supply three nearby cafés every morning
options.feedback: Recipes, ovens and bakers carry over. New are business buyers, early deliveries and lower prices per loaf. One or two steps from the core.
New product format, new customers, new channel: freezing, packaging, couriers and online marketing. Possible, but three or four steps out.

options.text: Sell lunch sandwiches made with her own bread
options.feedback: Same shop, same regulars, a new product. One step away, though it adds a lunch rush and food-prep work.

choice.afterReveal: A and C are adjacent moves; B is far from the core. The better pick is the step whose new piece Ana can learn most cheaply.

cards.title: Count the steps from the core.
body: An **adjacent move** keeps most of what a business already does well and changes only one or two things. For café wholesale, Ana writes two lists:
list: **Carries over:** recipes, ovens, bakers, her reputation
**New:** business customers, 6 a.m. deliveries, wholesale prices
cards.callout: Two new pieces is adjacent. Five new pieces is a different business.
cards.softwareNote: The same count works for software: a new customer type, a new sales channel or a new technical skill each counts as a step away from the core.

cards.title: Close moves can hide one hard piece.
body: Wholesale looks like "just more bread." But cafés pay less per loaf than walk-in customers, and they need it on time every day. One late delivery can lose the account.
Staying close also has a ceiling: one neighborhood only eats so much bread. Adjacent moves lower risk; they don't remove it. Name the new piece and test it small, say with one café for a month.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app.
body: Your app handles appointments for dental clinics. Most clinics in your city already use it, so selling more of the same is slowing down. Your team can take on one new move this year.

options.text: Sell the same app to veterinary clinics
options.feedback: Market development, and adjacent: the same product for buyers with the same appointment job. The main new piece is learning a new set of customers.

options.text: Add insurance billing for your dental clinics
options.feedback: Product development for loyal users, which is a real strength. But billing rules are a whole new skill, so it's further from your core than it looks.

options.text: Launch a table-booking app for restaurants
options.feedback: New product, new customers, new way of selling: close to diversification. It shares the word "booking" and little else.

cards.title: Grow from what already works, one step at a time.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Four ways to grow** sorted options by new products and new customers. **Core and adjacent moves** counted how many new pieces each option needed.
**Try it today:** write down three growth ideas. Next to each, list what carries over and what's new. Look hardest at the one with the shortest "new" list.
